conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you tonight. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi… I was in a car accident two days ago. A car ran a red light and hit me head-on. The airbag went off, and I blacked out for a second.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Did you go to the ER then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I drove myself. They did a CT scan and said no bleeding in my head or broken neck. I had a burn on my left wrist from the airbag. They sent me home with pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And since then, what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My headache got worse. It’s in my forehead, really bad, and I started vomiting—yellow fluid, not bloody. I couldn’t keep anything down, not even water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds rough. And you said you couldn’t take your medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. I haven’t taken my prednisone, Florinef, or Synthroid since the accident. I just couldn’t keep them down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. You have Addison’s disease, so missing those steroid doses can be dangerous. We’ll get you back on them safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried about that. My PCP told me to come back to the ER, so I did.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good call. We’ve started you on IV fluids and gave you some Dilaudid for the pain. How’s the headache now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better since the medicine, but it still hurts a lot. It’s worse with light and noise. I had to ask for earplugs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds like a migraine. Given the accident, it could also be a post-concussion headache. But your repeat CT was clean, so no bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had migraines before, years ago. This feels similar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also gave you an injection of hydrocortisone to cover your Addison’s. You’ll get another dose soon, then switch back to your oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes me feel better. But the Dilaudid gives me the creeps—like I’m jittery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ll note that. We can try other pain meds as your nausea improves. For now, we’re also giving Zofran for nausea through the IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Headache’s still there, but maybe a bit less. I haven’t vomited since last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’re going to keep you on IV fluids and slowly see if you can start drinking. Maybe some clear liquids later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like that. I’m really thirsty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray and ECG this morning—both normal. No heart or lung issues from the accident.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I was worried about that too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back—electrolytes are stable, kidney function is good, and your blood count is where it usually is.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing’s really wrong besides the headache and vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your exam is normal, no signs of infection or abdominal issues. We think it’s migraine-related, worsened by stress and missing your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My neck is still stiff. And I had a muscle spasm earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s common after a crash. The neck tenderness is likely from muscle strain. We can add something mild for spasms if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been able to sip water and ginger ale without vomiting. That’s great. We’re switching you to oral anti-nausea meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel like I might actually eat something soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re now on your regular prednisone and Florinef by mouth. We’ll stop the IV steroids. Your blood pressure is stable—good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad I’m back on my meds. I was scared I’d get an adrenal crisis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did the right thing coming in. Missing those doses with vomiting is risky. But you’re back on track now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you slept through the night, no vomiting, and you ate toast and applesauce. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great. But what if the headache comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending you home with your regular migraine meds. If the headache returns, try your usual routine. Use acetaminophen at night if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—should I keep taking them all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly as before. We’re increasing your Celexa to 20 mg for depression. And keep using the hydrocortisone injection if you’re sick or can’t take pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And when should I worry enough to come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If your headache gets worse, or you have vision changes, weakness, fever, or can’t keep fluids down, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You can go home in a couple of hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home and rest in a quiet room.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check—you’re tolerating food, walking fine, and your pain is manageable. All set for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I was really scared, but you’ve helped a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy, follow up with your PCP, and call if anything changes.
